_description: Continuity Audit (L10) eval-harness fixture, manuscript 2 of the medium set (LOOM_CONTINUITY_AUDIT.md §21). 'The Ash Court' — an 11-scene secondary-world fantasy of court succession, with 12 planted contradictions across all four audited classes plus 4 precision-control non-errors. Longer than manuscript 1 so the planted errors sit further apart and the prose reads more naturally. gold_claims score per-scene extraction recall; gold_pairs score pairwise adjudication; gold_contradictions are the end-to-end findings the pipeline should surface.
title: The Ash Court

scenes.title: The Mountain Road
scenes.prose: Lirien came up the mountain road on the eighth day of riding, saddle-sore and silent, the silver ring of office cold on one finger. An envoy of the Riverlands was a small thing in the eyes of a mountain court, and Lirien meant to be a careful one. Cael Doran rose ahead, a city of grey stone stacked against the peak, and at its north gate the Ash Tower stood black and branchless above the wall. Below the walls the river ran east, swollen with snowmelt, loud enough to be heard from the road. The gate-guards took Lirien's name and the Riverlands seal without warmth. Inside, the streets climbed. Somewhere a bell was tolling, slow, the way a bell tolls for the dying and not the dead. Lirien had been sent to witness a succession, and it seemed the kingdom did not mean to make it easy.

scenes.title: The Steward
scenes.prose: The steward met Lirien in an antechamber hung with old hunting tapestries. Vael was a stooped, dry man with ink-stained fingers, and he had served three kings of Cael Doran in his long life. 'You'll have come for the succession,' he said. 'King Bren has been five winters dead, and his widow holds the court only until the matter is settled.' He led Lirien up, and up — the throne room of Cael Doran lay on the topmost floor of the keep, a cold hall close under the roof-slates, reached by a stair that turned and turned. 'The Queen will see you,' Vael said, 'though she tires quickly now.' He paused at the door. 'Say little. This court listens to everything and forgives nothing.'

scenes.title: The Queen's Gallery
scenes.prose: Queen Areth received the envoy not on the throne but in a long gallery, walking its length slowly with one hand along the rail. She was thin as a reed, and her eyes were a pale, washed grey, and they missed nothing. 'The Riverlands send a watcher,' she said. 'Good. Let them watch.' Down the gallery hung the banners of the great houses, and above the Queen's own door the green banner of House Doran stirred in the draught — green for the mountain pine, Lirien had been taught as a child. Areth could still walk, still climb the gallery stair on a clear morning, though Vael hovered always a pace behind her. 'My husband's seat will not stay empty long,' the Queen said. 'There are those who would fill it before I am even gone.'

scenes.title: Ser Caud
scenes.prose: Ser Caud commanded what remained of the household guard, and he found Lirien on the walls at dusk. He was a big man going grey, and an old sword-scar ran up through his left eyebrow and lost itself in his hairline. 'An envoy,' he said, testing the word. 'You'll be reporting home, then, whatever happens here.' 'Witnessing,' Lirien said. 'There is a difference.' Caud grunted. He had the look of a man who had backed a side already and did not love his choice. 'The Princess is the heir by blood,' he said. 'Remember that, Riverlander, however the wind blows in the lower halls.' Then he was gone along the rampart, and the cold came down off the peak after him.

scenes.title: The Feast to Come
scenes.prose: The lower halls of Cael Doran were warmer and far less honest. Lirien took a cup of spiced wine by the great hearth and listened. The talk was all of the Feast of Embers — the kingdom's oldest festival, and a month away yet, though already the kitchens smoked day and night. 'The succession will be cried at the Feast,' a wine-merchant confided. 'Always the way. A crown looks better by firelight.' An envoy of the Riverlands, Lirien said little and missed nothing, which was the whole of the office. A serving-girl refilled the cup unasked. In a month, then, the question would be answered one way or another — and a month, in a court like this one, was a great deal of time.

scenes.title: Whispers
scenes.prose: Past midnight, a page brought Lirien a folded note and no name. The corridor it led to was dark and smelled of tallow. There Lirien waited, and no one came, and at last went back unsatisfied. But in the morning, asked by Vael how the night had passed, Lirien said a careless thing: 'I had not thought the old King's death was so quiet a poisoning.' The steward's ink-stained hand went still on the ledger. The word had not been spoken aloud in Cael Doran — not once, not by anyone — and Lirien had no leave to know it. 'Who told you that,' Vael said, and it was not a question, and there was no longer any warmth in the dry old voice at all.

scenes.title: The Princess
scenes.prose: Princess Sibba kept her own rooms in the east wing, and she received Lirien with the crimson banner of House Doran hung behind her chair — crimson, for the blood-right she meant everyone to remember. She was young and quick-eyed and entirely unfrightened. 'My mother thinks me a child,' she said. 'The court thinks me a girl. You will write home what you see, envoy, and what you see is the rightful heir.' Lirien, with a fortnight's hard riding still aching in both knees, only bowed. 'I never go up to that cold Ash Tower,' Sibba added, lightly, when the talk turned to where the old conspiracies had been hatched. 'Draughty, haunted places. Leave them to the crows.' She smiled, and the smile did not reach her quick eyes at all.

scenes.title: The Map Room
scenes.prose: Vael's clerks kept a map room low in the keep, and Lirien was permitted an hour there, ostensibly to trace the Riverlands' own borders. The great map of Cael Doran was painted on a table the size of a bed. The grey city climbed its mountain just as Lirien had first seen it from the road, every street and stair set down in faded ink. The river ran west of the walls on the map, a blue thread curling away toward the lowlands. And the Ash Tower — Lirien set a finger on it — stood at the south gate, marked with a small black flame. A clerk watched from the doorway, and so Lirien traced the Riverlands border dutifully and remembered the rest.

scenes.title: The Reveal
scenes.prose: It was Vael, in the end, who told Lirien the truth, because a frightened man will sometimes speak to a stranger what he cannot say to a friend. They stood in the cold map room after the clerks had gone. 'King Bren did not die of the lung-fever they cried in the streets,' the steward said. 'He was poisoned. Three winters ago, at his own table, and the court has buried the word ever since.' He said it the way a man sets down a stone he has carried too far. 'Three winters,' Lirien said softly, 'and no one tried for it.' 'No one living dares,' said Vael. So there it was, spoken aloud at last — and Lirien thought of a careless sentence said over a ledger days before, and understood how badly it had been timed.

scenes.title: The Tower
scenes.prose: Lirien climbed the Ash Tower at last, on the night before the Feast, and found it not empty. Princess Sibba was already there at the top, a lamp at her feet, as though the cold haunted place were a second home to her. Ser Caud stood with her — and in the lamp-light the old sword-scar showed plain, running up through his right eyebrow into the grey hair. They did not send Lirien away. 'You have seen us, then,' Sibba said. 'Write that down too.' On Lirien's hand the envoy's ring caught the light, a dull worn bronze. Below, through the tower's one window, the lights of the Queen's gallery still burned; Areth, they said, no longer slept at all.

scenes.title: Embers
scenes.prose: The Feast of Embers was three days hence when the court assembled — three days, and the kingdom already smelled of woodsmoke and waiting. The succession was cried not in the high cold hall under the slates but in the throne room at the foot of the great stair, where the whole court might press in to hear it. Vael read the proclamation in his dry voice; he had served two kings of Cael Doran, and his hands did not shake. Queen Areth did not come down. She kept to her bed now, too weak to rise, and when Lirien was brought up to take her leave the Queen's dark eyes found the envoy's face one last time. 'Watch,' she said again, as she had at the first. 'And remember it kindly, if you can.' Then Lirien rode down the mountain road, and behind, the bells of Cael Doran began at last to ring.
